I think this is actually one of the most underrated uses. Science has become so specialized that even within physics, people working on adjacent problems often speak slightly different languages. I work on black holes, on things like the photon ring and what we can learn from imaging them, and it constantly turns out that the mathematical structure I need was worked out decades ago by someone in a completely different area, maybe in optics, or in dynamical systems, or in some corner of pure math. The bottleneck has never really been intelligence; it's been knowing that the thing exists and knowing what it's called.

That's where a tool like ChatGPT is really valuable. You can describe your problem in your own vocabulary, in a messy, half-formed way, and it can say, "This looks a lot like such-and-such in another field, and here's how people there think about it." That kind of translation used to depend on luck: bumping into the right colleague at a conference, or happening to sit next to a mathematician at lunch. Now you can have that conversation whenever you want.

Of course, you still have to check everything. It sometimes makes connections that sound plausible but don't hold up. But even then, it gives you a lead to follow. In research, a good pointer to the right literature can save you weeks or months, and sometimes it changes the way you see the whole problem. So I see it less as a replacement for expertise and more as a bridge between expertises, and I think that's where some of the most interesting science happens.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I'm a theoretical physicist, and most of my work is on black holes, the kind of thing you'd test with the Event Horizon Telescope or future space missions. And one thing you learn pretty quickly in that line of work is that the hard problems almost never stay inside your own field. You hit a question about plasma physics, or about signal processing, or about some corner of pure mathematics, and you realize the answer probably exists already, written by someone who speaks a completely different dialect.

That translation problem is where I've found ChatGPT genuinely useful. Historically, the way you crossed into a neighboring field was you found a friend in that department, took them to lunch, and spent an hour asking what probably felt to them like very naive questions. That works, but it's slow, and there's a social cost. You don't want to burn a colleague's afternoon on something that might be a dead end.

With ChatGPT, I can be as naive as I need to be, at eleven at night, with no embarrassment. I can say, here's the object I care about, here's roughly what I think I need, what does this look like in your language? And it will tell me, oh, what you're describing is basically a well-studied thing in optics, or in applied math, and here's the vocabulary people use for it. Once I have the right words, I'm back in familiar territory. I can go read the actual papers, I can check things myself, I can go find the real expert and have a much higher-quality conversation with them.

I want to be careful not to oversell it. It's not doing the physics for me, and I wouldn't trust it on the fine details without verifying. But the bottleneck in interdisciplinary work was rarely the fine details. It was knowing that a bridge existed at all, and knowing what the bridge was called. For that, it's turned something that used to take weeks of searching and asking around into something that takes an evening. And I think the cumulative effect of that, across a lot of scientists, could be pretty significant, because so many of the interesting ideas live right at those boundaries between fields.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most useful things it can do is help us cross vocabulary barriers. You can know your own field very well and still struggle to read a paper in a neighboring field, because people use different language, emphasize different questions, and take different things for granted.

With ChatGPT, you can describe the problem you’re working on and ask, “Does this resemble something people study elsewhere? What would they call it?” That can give you a starting point—a connection you might otherwise never have thought to look for.

Of course, you still have to check whether the connection is real. But helping you formulate the right question, or understand enough of another field to have a productive conversation with an expert, is already enormously valuable.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of science comes down to finding the right connection. You can spend years working on a problem in your own language, while someone in a neighboring field has developed exactly the tool you need—but calls it something completely different. You might never find it because you don’t know what to search for.

That’s where I see a lot of value in ChatGPT: you can describe what you’re trying to do and ask, “Does this resemble anything in another field? How would a mathematician formulate this? What would a computer scientist call it?” It can help you learn enough of that language to start reading the literature and talking to the right people.

Of course, you still have to check whether the connection actually works. But helping scientists discover which conversations they should be having—that could be enormously useful.
